listing_view.reasoning: Subscription built from ~0.35x on day one to 5.86x by the final afternoon, with the bulk arriving on the last day [demand — figures given to me], which is typical late retail/HNI buying and suggests a chance of a decent debut. But I have no grey market data, no anchor book, and no basis to judge pricing versus peers, so 68 is as far as the evidence supports.

longterm_view.reasoning: Revenue grew 61% CAGR and PAT 72% CAGR over two years with an order book that rose from ₹3,914 mn to ₹9,166 mn [business, page 205; business, page 207], so the top-line story is real on paper. But operating cash flow was negative in all three years (−₹334 mn, −₹7,654 mn, −₹965 mn — figures given to me) and nearly 30% of incremental sales growth is uncollected receivables, meaning reported profit is not arriving as cash; nothing in the extracts given to me explains this, so the accounting-to-cash gap is unexplained rather than benign.

governance.reasoning: Extracts show only boilerplate: promoter benefits confined to disclosed related-party transactions [promoters, page 258] and a claim of no supplier conflicts [promoters, page 259], which is seller self-description, not evidence of good or bad conduct. No adverse finding is visible either, hence neutral.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Operating cash flow is negative in all three years despite ₹4,143 mn PAT in the latest year, so earnings quality is unproven and the model consumes cash as it grows (figures given to me).

key_risks.risk: Growth partly funded by not getting paid
key_risks.why_it_matters: 29.6% of incremental revenue is receivables growth, so a meaningful slice of the 44% latest-year growth is sales billed but not collected (figures given to me).
The company itself describes its industry as having entry-barrier and competitive pressure, so the reported growth depends on continuously winning fresh orders at defensible margins.
With negligible debt and persistently negative free cash flow, the raise is what funds working capital; dilution, not operations, is paying for the growth (figures given to me).

answers.question: check whether the growth is organic and repeatable
answers.answer: Partly supported but not proven. The order book grew from ₹3,914 mn to ₹6,874 mn to ₹9,166 mn [business, page 205; business, page 207] and the document attributes this to pre-qualification credentials and execution track record [business, page 207], which is consistent with organic contract wins. However, ~30% of sales growth is uncollected receivables and cash flow is negative throughout (figures given to me), so repeatability at acceptable cash economics is not established. The document's own competitive warning [business, page 221] undercuts the seller's own repeatability claim.

answers.question: veto — how is the business funded?
answers.answer: Largely by equity and customer credit, not by operations or debt. Total borrowings are trivial (₹232 mn latest, negative net in prior years) while net worth jumped from ₹4,957 mn to ₹15,678 mn over two years, indicating fresh equity infusions funded the balance sheet; meanwhile operations consumed cash (figures given to me). This IPO looks like the next tranche of that external funding. That is a genuine concern but not an automatic veto, since the order book is real.

answers.question: negative operating cash flow in all three years — is there an explanation in the document?
answers.answer: Not in the extracts I was given. Nothing in the litigation, governance, or business passages I received discusses cash flow, working capital cycles, or receivable recovery timelines — the only related claim is that order book growth 'reinforces financial and operational stability' [business, page 207], which says nothing about cash. The hard stop stands unless the full document's working capital discussion (not provided to me) shows a short, credible receivable cycle.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A working-capital section in the full prospectus showing contractual receivable cycles that are shortening, plus proof the latest year's receivables were collected post-period, would upgrade the long-term view materially. Conversely, disclosure that growth came from a small set of related or government clients, or that the fresh-issue portion is being used mainly to repay promoter-linked obligations, would push it lower.
